title: System Design for Next-Gen Frontier Models — Dylan Patel, SemiAnalysis

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is serving inference workloads—prefill vs decode, continuous batching, disaggregated prefill, context caching, and inference engines like vLLM and TensorRT-LLM. The content addresses cross-domain AI infrastructure and the tools/platforms builders use for inference serving and training at scale. Covers production inference serving deployment and next-generation GPU training infrastructure. Requires prior understanding of LLM inference pipelines, GPU memory-bandwidth tradeoffs, batching, and distributed training. Recorded live conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Multiple direct transcript excerpts with specific technical claims about inference systems strongly support the classification.

summary: Patel opens addressing perceived model stagnation—current top models are 2022-era architectures trained longer. He breaks inference into prefill (compute-intensive: 2K prompt = 1 PFLOP, 32K = 20 PFLOPs) and decode (memory-bandwidth-intensive: must load all weights per token). Serving GPT-4 at 30 tokens/sec for 64 users needs ~60 TB/s vs. H100's ~3 TB/s. This asymmetry drives 3-4x input/output token pricing. Llama 405B is the open-source capability unlock but requires TensorRT-LM or vLLM, not llama.cpp. Continuous batching is essential (batch size 1 is 10-100x more expensive). Disaggregated prefill separates workloads onto different accelerator pools to isolate noisy neighbors and protect time-to-first-token SLAs. Context caching (Google's Gemini 1.5 Pro, 2M context) avoids KV cache recomputation—critical for enterprise use cases where prefill dominates cost. vLLM is building open-source context caching, storing KV cache on CPU memory or storage rather than GPU memory. Patel then pivots to next-generation training infrastructure. GPT-4 required 20,000 chips for 90-100 days (~38 GWh); current 100,000 GPU clusters from OpenAI, xAI, and Anthropic could train GPT-4 in 3 days. Next-gen models will have tens of trillions of parameters with 10e26-10e27 training flops (vs. GPT-4's ~2e25), requiring 200+ GB/s memory bandwidth to serve. Microsoft's Arizona GPT-5 data center has ~100,000 GPUs at 150 megawatts; Elon plans a 300,000 GPU cluster with ~$500M/year power costs and cluster costs exceeding $10 billion. At this scale, fully connected clusters become impossible, and optical transceiver failures (~5-year lifespan) cause failures every ~5 minutes at 500K GPU scale. The Silicon Lottery means chips vary in performance; synchronous training means one slower GPU slows the entire cluster. ByteDance documented a 25% speed decrease from a single underperforming GPU on a 20,000 GPU cluster. Patel closes noting AGI hopes rest on 100x compute reducing hallucinations, and that many inference strategies labs use for Llama 405B-class models aren't yet in open source.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Model Stagnation and Next-Generation Scale
sections.summary: Patel addresses perceived model stagnation, explaining current models are 2022-era training with smaller models trained longer. GPT-4 at ~1.8T parameters, ~200B active per token, ~600 GFLOPs/token will soon be considered last-generation as larger models arrive. He pivots to inference as the practical focus for builders.

sections.title: Inference Fundamentals: Prefill vs Decode
sections.summary: Inference has two distinct workloads: prefill (compute-intensive prompt processing—2K prompt = 1 PFLOP, 32K prompt = 20 PFLOPs) and decode (memory-bandwidth-intensive iterative token generation requiring loading all model weights per token). Serving GPT-4 at 30 tokens/sec for 64 users needs ~60 TB/s bandwidth vs. H100's ~3 TB/s, a severe systems challenge.

sections.title: Pricing Economics and Open-Source Inference
sections.summary: The compute vs. bandwidth asymmetry drives a 3-4x pricing ratio: $5/M input, $15/M output for best models. Llama 405B is the open-source capability unlock but cannot run on llama.cpp—needs TensorRT-LM (Nvidia) or vLLM (AMD/Intel). Continuous batching is essential as batch size 1 is 10-100x more expensive.

sections.title: Disaggregated Prefill and Noisy Neighbors
sections.summary: Disaggregated prefill separates prefill and decode onto different accelerator pools. Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic publicly use this; Together and Fireworks hint at it. It addresses noisy neighbors—malicious queries can trivially slow services, impacting time-to-first-token. Patel argues rate limits are not the correct solution.

sections.title: Context Caching as Fine-Tuning Alternative
sections.summary: Google's context caching for Gemini 1.5 Pro (2M context) avoids recomputing KV cache each query. Critical for enterprise use cases where prefill dominates API cost. Fine-tuning best models is impossible or prohibitively expensive; context caching with long context is a practical alternative. Open-source equivalents are coming.

sections.title: Open-Source Context Caching and Next-Gen Cluster Scale
sections.summary: vLLM is building open-source context caching, storing KV cache on CPU memory or storage rather than GPU memory. Patel then pivots to next-gen training: GPT-4 used 20,000 chips for 90-100 days (~38 GWh); new 100,000 GPU clusters (OpenAI, xAI, Anthropic) could train it in 3 days. Next-gen models will have tens of trillions of parameters, requiring 200+ GB/s bandwidth. Microsoft's Arizona GPT-5 site has ~100,000 GPUs at 150 MW; Elon plans 300,000 GPUs (~$500M/year power, $10B+ cluster). At scale, fully connected clusters are impossible, optical transceivers fail every ~5 minutes at 500K GPU scale, and the Silicon Lottery means one slow GPU slows synchronous training—ByteDance saw 25% slowdown from one GPU on a 20K cluster.
